name: Root element and namespaces
desc: Every FXML file has one root element. It carries the default JavaFX namespace and the fx namespace, and usually names the controller.
example:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<?import javafx.scene.layout.BorderPane?>

<!-- One root. Both namespaces go here and are inherited by children. -->
<BorderPane xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/17"
            xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1"
            fx:controller="sample.MainController">
    <!-- children are added to the parent in document order -->
</BorderPane>
body:
The default namespace value is the JavaFX version the file was written for. The runtime does not enforce it strictly, but keep it near your JDK level (`8`, `11`, `17`, `21`).

Without `xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1"` the parser rejects every `fx:` attribute before the loader runs, so a file that looks fine in an editor fails on startup.

A root must be a class with a no argument constructor. Interfaces, abstract classes and `Node` itself cannot be roots.

name: <?import ...?>
desc: Declares the class behind a short element name. One processing instruction per class, placed above the root element.
example:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>

<?import javafx.scene.control.Label?>
<?import javafx.scene.control.TextField?>
<?import javafx.scene.layout.HBox?>

<HBox xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/17"
      xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1" spacing="8">
    <Label text="City"/>
    <TextField fx:id="cityField"/>
</HBox>
body:
Attribute values that name a class, such as `fx:controller="sample.LoginController"`, use the fully qualified name and need no import. So do enum values written bare, like `fontWeight="BOLD"`, as long as the compiler import for the enum type exists.

Wildcards work (`<?import javafx.scene.control.*?>`), and they hide the mistake you are hunting: a typo inside a wildcard package fails as `ClassNotFoundException` at load time with no useful line number. Write the explicit imports in exam answers.

name: fx:id
desc: Registers a node in the loader namespace, sets the node id, and matches a controller field by name.
example:
<?import javafx.scene.control.Label?>
<?import javafx.scene.layout.VBox?>

<!-- The label is injected into the controller field named totalLabel. -->
<VBox xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/17" xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1">
    <Label fx:id="totalLabel" text="0.00"/>
</VBox>
body:
The value must be a valid Java identifier. `fx:id="total label"` or `fx:id="total.label"` is a parse error.

`fx:id` also sets the node's `id` property, so CSS can select `#totalLabel`. That id selector is fine for a one off; a style class is better when several nodes share a look.

A typo does not throw. The field simply stays null and the failure appears where you use it, which is why the name is the first thing to check when a controller field is unexpectedly null.

name: fx:controller
desc: Names the class that receives the injected nodes and handles the events. The loader instantiates it with a no argument constructor.
example:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<?import javafx.scene.layout.VBox?>

<VBox xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/17"
      xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1"
      fx:controller="sample.LoginController">
    <!-- sample.LoginController must be public and have a public no arg constructor -->
</VBox>
body:
The class needs a constructor the loader can call without arguments. A controller that only has `LoginController(Repository repo)` cannot be named here: use `setControllerFactory` on the loader instead.

In a modular project the controller package must be opened to `javafx.fxml` (`opens sample to javafx.fxml;`). Without it the class is loaded but reflection is refused, and the error reads like a missing class.

name: Controller field for fx:id
desc: Injects the node whose fx:id equals the field name. Public fields work too; @FXML allows private ones.
body:
The declared type must be assignable from the node in the FXML. A `Label` field for a `TextField` element fails during load.

Injection order inside one load: objects constructed, ids stored, fields injected, then `initialize()`. That is why a field read in the constructor is null and a field read in `initialize()` is ready.

A private field without `@FXML` is skipped without a warning. This is the single most common null pointer in FXML code.

name: initialize()
desc: Runs once per load, after field injection and before load() returns. Wiring belongs here, layout does not.
body:
The method may be private. It runs again for every new load, so each new controller starts from a clean state.

The nodes exist but the scene does not: `getScene()` returns null and control sizes are usually zero. Code that needs real measurements goes into `Platform.runLater(...)` or a listener on the scene.

The `Initializable` interface offers `initialize(URL location, ResourceBundle resources)` and still works. Implementing it and also writing an annotated `initialize()` calls both, in an order not worth relying on. Pick one.

name: onAction="#handler"
desc: Connects a control event to a controller method. The handler may take no arguments or one event argument.
example:
<?import javafx.scene.control.Button?>
<?import javafx.scene.layout.HBox?>

<!-- The # prefix means: look this name up in the controller -->
<HBox xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/17" xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1"
      fx:controller="sample.ToolbarController">
    <Button text="Save" onAction="#save"/>
    <Button text="Cancel" onAction="#cancel"/>
</HBox>

name: FXMLLoader.load(URL)
desc: Static helper that builds the tree and returns the root. It gives no access to the controller.
body:
The static call creates its own loader internally, so `getController()` is out of reach. When the screen needs data, a reference for navigation, or a resource bundle, use a `new FXMLLoader(...)` instead.

`load()` throws `IOException` for a missing file, bad XML, or a broken controller. It does not throw for a null URL: that fails with a message about the location not being set.

name: new FXMLLoader(...).load()
syntax: FXMLLoader loader = new FXMLLoader(url); Parent root = loader.load();
desc: The instance form. Use it when you need the controller, a controller factory, or a resource bundle.
body:
A loader is single use in practice. A second `load()` on the same instance rebuilds the tree and creates a second controller, so per screen means per loader.

`load()` returns the root, typed by the FXML root element. Assign it to `Parent` for a scene, or to the concrete type when you need its methods before adding it to the scene.

name: getClass().getResource(path)
desc: Resolves a file from the classpath. A leading slash starts at the classpath root; without it, resolution starts in the caller's package.

name: loader.getController()
desc: Returns the controller instance created during the load, so data and callbacks can be handed to it.
body:
The method returns null before `load()` finished, and also when the FXML has no `fx:controller` and no controller was set. Call it only after a successful load.

Because `initialize()` already ran, a setter called here must render the data itself. It cannot expect `initialize()` to pick it up later.

The generic form `loader.<ProfileController>getController()` avoids a cast in code that cannot use a typed local variable.

name: loader.setControllerFactory()
desc: Supplies controller instances from code, which allows constructor arguments when initialize() needs the data.
body:
Returning a subclass of the requested type is fine. Returning an unrelated object throws `ClassCastException` during the load.

The factory is the right tool when `initialize()` needs the data to build a table model or fill a list. The setter approach from `getController()` runs too late for that.

Do not combine it with `setController(...)` on the same loader, and do not expect the factory to override an `fx:controller` class with a different type.

name: <fx:include>
desc: Splices another FXML file into the tree. With fx:id, the parent controller gets both the child root and the child controller.
example:
<?import javafx.scene.layout.BorderPane?>

<BorderPane xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/17"
            xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1"
            fx:controller="sample.MainController">

    <!-- Loaded while the parent is built, with its own controller and initialize() -->
    <bottom>
        <fx:include fx:id="statusBar" source="status-bar.fxml"/>
    </bottom>
</BorderPane>

name: <fx:root type="...">
desc: Builds into an existing instance instead of a new one, so a node subclass can be its own controller.
body:
The FXML root element is `<fx:root type="javafx.scene.layout.HBox">` and the file has no `fx:controller` attribute. The instance passing `setController(this)` is the controller, which is how a typed constructor survives.

Setting both `fx:controller` and `setController` fails with a controller already specified error. With `fx:root` the attribute is always the wrong choice.

This pattern is useful for list rows, table cells and small reusable widgets; it is overkill for a screen.

name: stylesheets and styleClass
desc: Attaches a stylesheet relative to the FXML file and adds CSS class names to a node.
example:
<?import javafx.scene.layout.VBox?>
<?import javafx.scene.control.Label?>

<!-- @app.css is resolved next to this file; styleClass takes a space separated list -->
<VBox xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/17" xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1"
      stylesheets="@app.css" styleClass="panel">

    <Label text="Signed in" styleClass="hint"/>
    <Label text="Wrong password" styleClass="hint error"/>
</VBox>
body:
From code, attach the sheet to the scene once so it survives `scene.setRoot(...)`:

```java
scene.getStylesheets().add(getClass().getResource("/css/app.css").toExternalForm());
```

`toExternalForm()` is not optional: `getStylesheets()` holds strings, and a `URL` does not compile there.

Inline `style="-fx-text-fill: red;"` wins over any sheet rule. Keep it for one off debugging, because it cannot be themed and it hides the rule from the CSS file.

name: Resource bundle keys
desc: Reads a string from the loader's resource bundle instead of hard coding it in the FXML.
example:
<?import javafx.scene.control.Button?>
<?import javafx.scene.layout.HBox?>

<HBox xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/17" xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1"
      fx:controller="sample.FormController">
    <Button text="%save.label" onAction="#save"/>
</HBox>

name: Switching screens with scene.setRoot()
desc: Replaces the visible screen while keeping the stage, its size, and the scene stylesheets.
body:
Building a new `Scene` per screen throws away the stylesheets and resets the size, which is why beginners end up re adding CSS on every screen.

Navigation belongs to whoever owns the stage. Controllers call one method such as `app.showLogin()` and never touch the stage themselves, so the title and the current screen have a single owner.

A second `Stage` is for dialogs and tool windows. For main navigation, swap the root.

name: LoadException and its causes
desc: The wrapper for nearly every FXML failure. The nested cause names the real problem.
body:
The frequent causes, in the order they appear in practice:

- `ClassNotFoundException`: missing or misspelled `<?import?>`, or a wrong class in `fx:controller`.
- location not set: `getResource` returned null, so the path, the slash, or the resource folder is wrong.
- null field later: `fx:id` and field name differ, the field is private without `@FXML`, or the node lives in another file.
- handler not resolved: the `onAction` method is missing, private without `@FXML`, or has a wrong parameter list.
- controller already specified: `setController` was called on a loader whose FXML has `fx:controller`.
- no default constructor: the controller named in `fx:controller` only has constructors with arguments.
- XML parse error: an unclosed tag, an unquoted attribute, or a raw `&` in text. Use `&`.
- access error in a modular project: the controller package is not opened to `javafx.fxml`.
